title: When Is Planning Adjusted? How Residents Can Comment on Plans
desc: When urban and rural plans are adjusted, how general and local adjustments differ, how residents can comment on a plan and for how long (2026).
summary: Cases of planning adjustment, the two types of adjustment (general and local), and the community's right to comment under the Law on Urban and Rural Planning.
body: A plot that is residential land today may be affected by a planning adjustment. Conversely, homeowners also have the right to comment when the plan for their area is prepared or adjusted. This article summarises Law on Urban and Rural Planning No. 47/2024/QH15, as amended by Law 144/2025/QH15.

Urban and rural planning has three levels: general planning, zoning planning and detailed planning (Clause 3, Article 3). Detailed planning is the level closest to each plot and sets the building line, number of floors and function of the plot.
Under Article 45, a plan may be adjusted in these cases:
An adjustment of the socio-economic development, national defence or security strategy, or of a higher-level plan, changes the content of the approved plan;
A project whose investment policy has been approved by the National Assembly or the Prime Minister affects land use or the architectural space of the area;
Changes in climate, geology, hydrology, natural disasters, or national defence and security requirements;
To serve national or community interests when the demand for land for technical or social infrastructure changes;
The plan cannot be implemented or has negative effects;
The boundary or some land use indicators of a plot need adjusting to carry out a project in an area that already has a detailed plan.

General adjustment: when the role, nature, function or scale of an urban area, commune or functional zone changes, or the boundary or structure of the whole planned area changes; carried out on the basis of a planning review (Clause 1, Article 46).

Local adjustment: when the adjustment does not change the nature, function, boundary or main planning solutions and does not overload infrastructure; the planning task need not be redone (Clause 2, Article 46).

The planning organisation prepares the local adjustment dossier and seeks opinions from related agencies and from the residential community in the adjusted area and in surrounding areas directly affected.
The appraisal body reviews the grounds, conditions and content of the adjustment.
The competent authority approves it; the decision must clearly state the content of the adjustment.
The planning records are updated and the content of the adjustment is announced.
5. How can residents comment, and for how long?
A plan must be put to state agencies, organisations, experts and the relevant residential community for comment (Clause 2, Article 37). For the residential community (Clause 7, Article 37):
Form: sending dossiers and documents for residents to comment in writing; posting and displaying them in public places; or other forms under the law on exercising democracy at the grassroots level.
Time: at least 20 days and not more than 30 days from the date the content for comment is made public.
The planning organisation must compile, accept and explain the comments; the report on acceptance and explanation must be publicly announced (Clause 8, Article 37).

No later than 15 days after approval, the plan must be publicly announced (Article 50). When a plan is adjusted, the boundary markers are adjusted accordingly (Clause 5, Article 52). Homeowners should follow notices at the commune- or ward-level People's Committee and recheck the plan before applying for a building permit; see Procedure for a building permit for a single-family house in 2026.

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. Law 47/2024/QH15 is partly expired because it has been amended by Law 71/2025/QH15 (not yet in our library) and Law 144/2025/QH15; some wording on the district level in the original law has been replaced following the 2-level local government reorganisation. Ask the commune- or ward-level People's Committee which plans are currently out for comment locally.
